# How modern AI models work {#sec-ch05}

Words like "deep learning" and "large language model" sound very complex. But they are built from four simple ideas. In this chapter we go through these four ideas, and then see why asking an LLM like ChatGPT to make a decision is not as simple as it looks.

::: {.goals}
- Understand layers, embeddings and attention in simple words.
- See why big models often become overconfident.
- Understand why getting a clean decision out of an LLM is difficult.
:::

## Idea one: layers can draw any shape

One artificial **neuron** is the same as the logistic regression from Chapter 2: it multiplies each clue by a weight, adds them up, and turns the total into a probability. But one neuron can only separate cases with a straight line.

Some problems need more. For example, activity can be suspicious when it is unusual in *any* direction: far too much or far too little. A straight line cannot separate the normal middle from the unusual edges.

![A toy problem. Blue dots are normal activity; red crosses surround them on every side. One neuron (left) can only draw a straight line through it. With a hidden layer of three neurons (middle) the boundary becomes a triangle; with twelve (right), close to a circle.](/figures/ch06/line-limit.pdf){#fig-line-limit}

The solution is to pass the clues through a layer of neurons first. Each neuron draws its own line, and the next neuron combines these lines. Three lines make a triangle; twelve lines make almost a circle (@fig-line-limit). A network with several such layers is called a **deep** network. Training works the same way as before: predict, measure the mistake, and adjust. The mistake is passed backwards through the layers to adjust each weight; this is called **backpropagation** [@rumelhart1986].

The big advantage of deep networks is that they can learn their own clues from raw data like images or text [@lecun2015]. But when we already have clean, useful numbers, a deep network adds little. In our example, a small network does about as well as simple logistic regression ({{< num ch06 k_small.log_loss f3 >}} against {{< num ch06 k_lr.log_loss f3 >}}).

::: {.keyidea}
**Use deep learning for messy data, and simple models for clean data.** Deep networks shine on images and text. On clean numbers, a simple model is often just as good and easier to trust.
:::

## Idea two: words as numbers

A computer can only calculate with numbers, so words must become numbers. The trick comes from the study of language: *we understand a word by the words around it.* "Phishing" and "fraud" appear in similar sentences, near words like "email", "link" and "password". If we turn each word into a short list of numbers based on its neighbours, words used in similar ways get similar lists. This list is called an **embedding**. Similar documents also get similar embeddings, and this is how AI search finds related text.

But embeddings capture what a text is *about*, not the exact numbers inside it. To an embedding, an alert with a threat score of 0.05 and one with 0.95 look almost the same. In our example, predicting from similar past alerts gives honest probabilities but weak ranking (AUC {{< num ch07 knn.auc f2 >}}, against {{< num ch07 lr.auc f2 >}} for logistic regression).

## Idea three: words that look at each other

"Invoice, not phishing" and "phishing, not invoice" have the same words but opposite meanings. **Attention** solves this. Each word looks at the other words in the sentence and decides which of them change its meaning. In "invoice, not phishing", the word "phishing" pays most attention to "not".

![What each word attends to after training. In "invoice not phishing", the word "phishing" puts nearly all its attention on "not". Nobody told the model about negation; it found that looking at the word before was the cheapest way to get the answers right.](/figures/ch08/heatmaps.pdf){#fig-heatmaps}

In @fig-heatmaps, nobody told the model about the word "not"; it learned this by itself. A model that only counts words reaches {{< num ch08 acc_bow pct >}} accuracy on this task, while attention reaches {{< num ch08 acc_att pct >}}.

A **transformer** is many attention layers stacked together [@vaswani2017]. There are two types. A **reader** sees the whole input at once, which suits understanding and deciding. A **writer** sees only the words before the current one, because it is producing text one word at a time. LLMs like ChatGPT are writers.

## Idea four: very large models, and a side effect

If we train a huge writer to guess the next word on a huge amount of text, it learns grammar, facts and some reasoning [@kaplan2020]. Then it is tuned with good example answers, and with feedback on which answers people prefer [@ouyang2022]. But people usually prefer answers that sound confident. OpenAI reported that GPT-4's confidence was well calibrated before this tuning and less calibrated after it [@openai2023].

![The same training run, on test alerts. Accuracy (left) barely moves. Log loss (middle) and calibration error (right) are flat for a while, then climb steeply. Watch only accuracy and you'd never notice.](/figures/ch09/overtraining.pdf){#fig-overtraining}

There is a deeper reason too. If we train a network that is much bigger than needed for too long, its accuracy hardly changes, but its calibration error grows from {{< num ch09 first.ece f3 >}} to {{< num ch09 last.ece f3 >}} (@fig-overtraining). Once the model gets most training cases right, the only way to improve its score further is to become more and more certain. It becomes certain about everything, even noise. Temperature scaling from Chapter 3 brings the error back to {{< num ch09 ece_after_T f3 >}}.

::: {.keyidea}
**Big models are often overconfident.** After long training, they say 99% too easily. Their probabilities must be checked and corrected before you use them.
:::

## How an LLM writes, and why this is a problem for decisions

![The generation loop. The model reads everything so far, produces a probability for every possible next token, one gets picked, it's appended, and the loop runs again.](/figures/ch10/loop.pdf){#fig-loop-06}

An LLM writes one small piece of text at a time, called a **token**. At each step, it gives a probability to every possible next token, picks one, adds it, and repeats (@fig-loop-06). This creates three problems for decisions.

**Longer answers take more time and money.** Each token waits for the previous one. In our example figures, a one-word answer takes about {{< num ch10 lat_1 f1 >}} seconds, but a long step-by-step answer takes about {{< num ch10 lat_1500 int >}} seconds.

**The same question can get different answers.** The model usually picks the next token with some randomness. In our example, out of forty borderline alerts asked twenty times each, {{< num ch10 n_split int >}} got different answers at different times.

**The answer is hidden inside text.** If we ask for the answer in a fixed format (JSON), some answers still come back broken, with extra chatting or with invented fields. "JSON mode" fixes the *format*, not the *correctness*: a model can still write "benign" for a real attack in perfect format.

![What came back when we asked for JSON, over 4,000 alerts. With only the prompt, some responses were wrapped in friendly chat, some were cut off mid-object, and some were valid JSON with a field nobody asked for. With JSON mode on, the first two problems vanish. The third doesn't.](/figures/ch11/json-failures.pdf){#fig-json-failures}

::: {.keyidea}
**A neat answer is not a correct answer.** An LLM can return a perfectly formatted "safe" for a real attack. Check the decision, not only the format.
:::

## Three kinds of "confidence"

Suppose an LLM replies: `"verdict": "malicious", "confidence": 0.95`. Can we trust this 0.95?

![Reliability of three "confidences" on the same test alerts, all reading the same raw text. The stated confidence barely separates attacks from harmless alerts. The token probability ranks well but is overconfident. The decision model ranks best and also sits close to the diagonal. Synthetic: an illustration, not a measurement of real models.](/figures/ch11/three-confidences.pdf){#fig-three-confidences}

- **The written confidence** is just text that the model wrote. In our example, the LLM used only {{< num ch11 n_distinct_stated int >}} different values, mostly 0.9 or more, so it hardly separates attacks from normal alerts.
- **The token probability** is the probability the model gave to the word "malicious". It ranks better but is overconfident, and it is the probability of a *word*, not of an answer.
- **A decision model's probability** is designed to be the probability of the answer itself (@fig-three-confidences). This is the gap that System One models try to fill.

::: {.exercises}
1. A company says its classifier is "97% accurate" and gives a confidence with every answer. You plan to act automatically when the confidence is above 0.9. What would you check first?
:::
